```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
options(digits=2)
require(tidyverse)
require(tigerstats)
require(lubridate)
kRdata <- read.csv(file = 'kRdata.csv')
kRdata <- kRdata %>%
mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor))
kData = kRdata
```
Data are from the Patient_Info dataset from South Korea 1 Jan to 1 May 2020. These data were retrieved from a downloadable zip file from kaggle.

Some of the data were uncoded for sex - sex must be just male or female.  77 of the data entries were coded sex as blank, so we omit these.  State of a patient must be died or alive - we adjust that as well.  This is done in the mutate function. 

Variables of interest: sex, result

Research Question: - Is dying independent of sex?

# Introduction
Using Kdata, can we determine that men and women are equally likely to die of covid 19 from data collected in South Korea through May 2019?

$H_A$ there is relationship between genders and death from covid 19 in South Korea in 2019.

$H_0$ there is no relationship between gender and death from covid 19 in south Korea in 2019.  

# Methods 

sex is categorical.  
result is categorical.   
 
# Data Results
## Graphical results    

```{r}
barchartGC(~result + sex,data=kData)
barchartGC(~result + sex,data=kData, type="percent")

```
the graph suggest that males are likely to die in comparison to females.

## Numerical results

```{r}
table1 <- xtabs(~result + Sex, data=kData)
rowPerc(table1)
colPerc(table1)
```
numerical result shows that 64% of males died compared to 36% of females, indicating that men are more likely to die faster.  

## Inferential results 

```{r}
chisq.test(table1)
chisqtestGC(table1)
fisher.test(table1)
```
the P value is less than .005     
we reject the Null hypothesis.     
And conclude that there is connection between sex and death from covid 19.
